section.title: The ooSQLite Class
section.para: The ooSQLite class has only class methods and class attributes, which are invoked on the class itself, as in .ooSQLite~libVersion. They deal with what belongs to the whole process rather than to a database: the defaults that new connections take, the version and the build options of SQLite, the memory that SQLite uses, and some utilities.
The class inherits from the ooSQLiteConstants class, so its constants can be used through it, as in .ooSQLite~OK. Most methods have a classic routine that does the same, named in each section.

section.title: null (Class attribute)
section.para: Reflects the default value that ooSQLite uses for SQL NULL values in the results of queries.

listitem.para: The current default: the .nil object, unless it has been changed, or a string.
The .nil object, or any other object, whose string value is then used: setting the attribute to 42 makes it the string 42.

The default is copied into each ooSQLiteConnection object when it is opened, and from the connection into each ooSQLiteStmt object when it is created: connections that are already open keep the value they have. The null attribute of a connection, and the null attribute of a statement, change it for that object only.
This attribute is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite feature.

This example makes NULL values appear as the string NULL in a new connection, and then restores the default:
.ooSQLite~null = 'NULL' conn = .ooSQLiteConnection~new(db~fileName) rows = conn~exec("SELECT name, price FROM foods WHERE type_id > 1;", .true) do row over rows say row['NAME']~left(8) row['PRICE']~right(5) end conn~close .ooSQLite~null = .nil /* Output: Bacon 3.75 Cheese NULL */

section.title: recordFormat (Class attribute)
section.para: Reflects the default format of the result sets that ooSQLite returns.

listitem.para: One of the result set format constants. The default is OO_ARRAY_OF_DIRECTORIES.
One of the result set format constants: OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS, OO_ARRAY_OF_DIRECTORIES, OO_STEM_OF_STEMS, or OO_CLASSIC_STEM. Raises a syntax error, 88.916, for any other value.

The formats are: OO_ARRAY_OF_DIRECTORIES, an Array with a Directory for each row, indexed by the names of the columns in uppercase; OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS, an Array whose first item is an Array with the names of the columns, followed by an Array of values for each row, so that row 1 is item 2; OO_STEM_OF_STEMS, a Stem whose tail 0 is the number of rows, and whose tails 1 to N are a Stem for each row, with a tail for each column; and OO_CLASSIC_STEM, a single Stem with the number of rows at tail 0 and the values at compound tails such as 1.NAME.

The default is copied into each ooSQLiteConnection object when it is opened, and from the connection into each ooSQLiteStmt object: connections that are already open keep the format they have. The format can be chosen for a connection, with the recordFormat attribute or the defFormat argument of new, for a statement, and for a single exec. Results that belong to no connection, such as those of the listBuiltins method of the ooSQLExtensions class, use this default.
This attribute is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite feature.

This example changes the default to an array of arrays. A connection that was already open, db, keeps the format 2, OO_ARRAY_OF_DIRECTORIES:
.ooSQLite~recordFormat = .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS conn = .ooSQLiteConnection~new(db~fileName) rows = conn~exec("SELECT id, name FROM foods WHERE type_id = 1;", .true) do row over rows say row[1]~left(3) row[2] end conn~close say 'Earlier connection:' db~recordFormat /* Output: id name 1 Bagels 2 Bagels, raisin Earlier connection: 2 */

section.title: &added11;zeroPointer (Class attribute)
section.para: Reflects a Pointer object whose value is zero, a null pointer.

listitem.para: A Pointer object whose isNull method returns true.
The Rexx programmer can not set the value of this attribute.

Some methods take a Pointer, the handle of a function or a data block of an external library. A null pointer is then the way to say "none": for example, the createCollation and collationNeeded methods of the ooSQLiteConnection class remove a collation or a handler from an external library when they are given the zero pointer. Rexx code has no other way to create a null Pointer.
This attribute is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite feature.
&added11;This attribute was in ooSQLite before version 1.1, but it was not documented.

This example registers the reverse collation of the exampleLibrary library, and removes it with the zero pointer:
.ooSQLExtensions~loadLibrary('examplelibrary') lib = .ooSQLExtensions~getLibrary('examplelibrary') say db~createCollation('reverse', lib~getHandle('reverse')) sql = "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE type_id = 1 ORDER BY name COLLATE reverse;" say db~exec(sql, .true)[1]['NAME'] say db~createCollation('reverse', .ooSQLite~zeroPointer) say db~exec(sql) say db~errMsg /* Output: 0 Bagels, raisin 0 257 no such collation sequence: reverse */

section.title: compileOptionGet (Class method)
section.para: Returns one of the options that were used at compile time when the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses was built.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
index [required]
The number of the option, 1 for the first one.
The option, without the SQLITE_ prefix, and with its value if it has one, such as THREADSAFE=1. For an index that is out of range, including 0 and negative numbers, the string NULL is returned.
The options are listed by increasing the index from 1 until NULL is returned. compileOptionUsed tests a single option.
Raises a syntax error, 88.907, if index is not a whole number.
The functionality of the compileOptionGet routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_compileoption_get API. The classic oosqlCompileOptionGet routine does the same.

This example displays the options that enable optional features. The list depends on how the library was built:
i = 1 do while .ooSQLite~compileOptionGet(i) \== 'NULL' option = .ooSQLite~compileOptionGet(i) if option~startsWith('ENABLE_') then say option i += 1 end /* Output might be: ENABLE_COLUMN_METADATA ENABLE_FTS3 ENABLE_FTS3_PARENTHESIS ENABLE_FTS4 ENABLE_FTS5 ENABLE_GEOPOLY ENABLE_MATH_FUNCTIONS ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT ENABLE_RTREE */

section.title: compileOptionUsed (Class method)
section.para: Tests if an option was used at compile time when the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses was built.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
name [required]
The name of the option, such as ENABLE_FTS5. The SQLITE_ prefix can be omitted, and the comparison is case insensitive. An option with a value can be given with it, as in THREADSAFE=1, to test the value too.
Returns true if the option was used, and false if it was not.

The options tell which optional features are in the library: full text search (ENABLE_FTS5), R*Tree indexes (ENABLE_RTREE), the math functions (ENABLE_MATH_FUNCTIONS), and others. compileOptionGet lists them all.
The functionality of the compileOptionUsed routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_compileoption_used API. The classic oosqlCompileOptionUsed routine does the same.

This example tests some options:
do option over .array~of('ENABLE_FTS5', 'ENABLE_RTREE', 'ENABLE_ICU', 'THREADSAFE=1') say option~left(14) .ooSQLite~compileOptionUsed(option) end /* Output: ENABLE_FTS5 1 ENABLE_RTREE 1 ENABLE_ICU 0 THREADSAFE=1 1 */

section.title: complete (Class method)
section.para: Tests if a text seems to form one or more complete SQL statements.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sql [required]
The text to test.
Returns true if the text ends with a complete statement, and false if more text is needed.

A statement is complete when it ends with a semicolon that is not inside a string, a quoted name, or a comment, and it is not the first part of a CREATE TRIGGER statement, which needs its END;. The statement is not parsed, so it can be complete and still have errors. The method is useful for programs that read SQL a line at a time, to know when to execute what they have read. Text with only white space and comments is not complete; a lone semicolon is.
The functionality of the complete routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_complete API. The classic oosqlComplete routine does the same.

This example joins lines until they form a complete statement. The semicolon inside the string of the second statement does not end it:
lines = .array~of("SELECT name", " FROM foods", " WHERE price > 2;", - "SELECT ';' AS semicolon;") sql = '' do line over lines sql = sql line if .ooSQLite~complete(sql) then do say 'Complete:' sql~space sql = '' end end /* Output: Complete: SELECT name FROM foods WHERE price > 2; Complete: SELECT ';' AS semicolon; */

section.title: &added11;encryptionAvailable (Class method)
section.para: Tells whether the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses can encrypt databases.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
Returns true if SQLite was built with an encryption extension, and false otherwise. The SQLite embedded in ooSQLite is built without one, so the method returns false.
The method tests the SQLITE_HAS_CODEC compile-time option, which the encryption extensions for SQLite used to define. Plain SQLite has no encryption.
This method is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API. The classic ooSQLiteEncryptionAvailable routine does the same.
&added11;This method was in ooSQLite before version 1.1, but it was not documented.

This example tests whether encryption is available:
say 'Encryption available:' .ooSQLite~encryptionAvailable /* Output: Encryption available: 0 */

section.title: &changed11;enquote (Class method)
section.para: Converts Rexx values into SQL literals, quoted and separated by commas, ready to be put in an SQL statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
values [optional]
A single value, or an Array of values. If it is omitted, the result is NULL.

A string with the values as SQL literals: each value is put between single quotes, with the single quotes inside it doubled, and the .nil object becomes NULL. For an Array, the literals are separated by a comma and a blank, and an index that has no item also becomes NULL; an empty Array gives NULL.

The number of values of an Array is its size, not its number of items, so that missing items stay in place as NULL. Every value is quoted, also numbers: SQLite converts a quoted number to a number when the column has numeric affinity.

Quoting the values protects an SQL statement built from data against SQL injection. Binding the values to the parameters of a prepared statement, with the bind methods of the ooSQLiteStmt class, does it without building the statement, and keeps the types of the values.

This method is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API. It uses the %Q format of SQLite's sqlite3_mprintf API. The classic ooSQLiteEnquote routine does the same, with a stem instead of an Array.
&changed11;Before ooSQLite 1.1, an Array of 7 or more items gave a result of at most 4095 characters, cut without an error when the last item went over. The result now has no length limit.

This example builds an INSERT statement with a value that contains a quote, and shows how an Array with a missing item, a single value, and no value are converted:
row = .array~new(4) row[1] = 'Tea' row[2] = "Earl Grey's" row[4] = .nil sql = "INSERT INTO foods(type_id, name, price, picture) VALUES(" || - .ooSQLite~enquote(.array~of(4, row[2])) || ", NULL, NULL);" say sql say db~exec(sql) say .ooSQLite~enquote(row) say .ooSQLite~enquote("It's a happy day!") say .ooSQLite~enquote /* Output: INSERT INTO foods(type_id, name, price, picture) VALUES('4', 'Earl Grey''s', NULL, NULL); 0 'Tea', 'Earl Grey''s', NULL, NULL 'It''s a happy day!' NULL */

section.title: &changed11;errStr (Class method)
section.para: Returns the English description of a result code.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
resultCode [required]
A Result Code, an extended result code, or an ooSQLite specific result code.
The description. For an extended result code, it is the description of its primary result code. For a number that is not a result code, it is unknown error.

The description does not need a connection. The errMsg method of the ooSQLiteConnection class returns the message of the last error of a connection, which is often more precise, such as no such table: food instead of SQL logic error.
Raises a syntax error, 88.907, if resultCode is not a whole number.

The functionality of the errStr routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_errstr API. The descriptions of the ooSQLite specific result codes are added by ooSQLite. The classic oosqlErrStr routine does the same.
&changed11;Before ooSQLite 1.1, the ooSQLite specific result codes 1005 to 1011 were described as unknown error.

This example describes some result codes:
codes = .array~of(.ooSQLite~OK, .ooSQLite~BUSY, .ooSQLite~CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE, - .ooSQLite~OO_NO_SUCH_PACKAGE, 5000) do code over codes say code~right(5)':' .ooSQLite~errStr(code) end /* Output: 0: not an error 5: database is locked 2067: constraint failed 1007: the package is not loaded 5000: unknown error */

section.title: libVersion (Class method)
section.para: Returns the version of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses, as a string.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The version, such as 3.52.0.

The SQLite library is embedded in the ooSQLite library, so this is the version that the ooSQLite library was built with. The VERSION constant of the ooSQLiteConstants class has the version that ooSQLite.cls was written for: if they differ, ooSQLite.cls and the library do not belong together. Note that .ooSQLite~VERSION invokes the version method, not the constant, because a method of the class takes precedence over a constant it inherits: use .ooSQLiteConstants~VERSION. The same holds for SOURCE_ID and VERSION_NUMBER, which have no method of their own, but are clearer with the class that defines them.
The functionality of the libVersion routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_libversion API. The classic oosqlLibVersion routine does the same.

This example checks that ooSQLite.cls and the library match:
if .ooSQLite~libVersion \== .ooSQLiteConstants~VERSION then say 'ooSQLite.cls does not match the ooSQLite library' else say 'SQLite' .ooSQLite~libVersion /* Output might be: SQLite 3.52.0 */

section.title: libVersionNumber (Class method)
section.para: Returns the version of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses, as a number.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The version as a whole number, X * 1000000 + Y * 1000 + Z for version X.Y.Z: 3052000 for 3.52.0.
A number is easier to compare than a string: it is the way to test whether a feature of SQLite is available. It matches the VERSION_NUMBER constant when ooSQLite.cls and the library belong together.
The functionality of the libVersionNumber routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_libversion_number API. The classic oosqlLibVersionNumber routine does the same.

This example uses a RETURNING clause only if SQLite supports it:
if .ooSQLite~libVersionNumber < 3035000 then say 'RETURNING clauses need SQLite 3.35.0 or later' else do rows = db~exec("DELETE FROM foods WHERE price IS NULL RETURNING name;", .true) say 'Deleted:' rows[1]['NAME'] end /* Output: Deleted: Cheese */

section.title: memoryHighWater (Class method)
section.para: Returns the largest number of bytes of memory that SQLite has used at any one time.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
reset [optional]
If true, the mark is set to the memory in use, as memoryUsed returns it, after its value is returned. The default is false.
The largest number of bytes in use at the same time since the process started, or since the mark was last reset. With reset, the value before the reset is returned.
The memory is that of the whole process, all the connections together. Resetting the mark before an operation and reading it after tells how much memory the operation needed at its peak.
Raises a syntax error, 34.901, if reset is not a logical value.
The functionality of the memoryHighWater routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_memory_highwater API. The classic oosqlMemoryHighWater routine does the same.

This example measures the memory that a query needs. The numbers depend on the system and the version of SQLite:
.ooSQLite~memoryHighWater(.true) -- the mark is now the memory in use before = .ooSQLite~memoryUsed sql = "WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM c" - "WHERE i < 10000) SELECT max(randomblob(i % 1000)) FROM c ORDER BY 1;" rows = db~exec(sql, .true) say 'In use before:' before say 'In use after: ' .ooSQLite~memoryUsed say 'Peak: ' .ooSQLite~memoryHighWater /* Output might be: In use before: 63688 In use after: 69016 Peak: 90784 */

section.title: memoryUsed (Class method)
section.para: Returns the number of bytes of memory that SQLite has in use.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The number of bytes that SQLite has allocated and not yet freed, for the whole process.
memoryHighWater returns the largest value it has had. The status method gives this and other figures about the memory of SQLite.
The functionality of the memoryUsed routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_memory_used API. The classic oosqlMemoryUsed routine does the same.
See the examples of memoryHighWater and releaseMemory.

section.title: releaseMemory (Class method)
section.para: Asks SQLite to free memory that it does not need, such as the pages of the databases that it keeps in its cache.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
nBytes [required]
The number of bytes to free.
The number of bytes that were freed, which can be more or less than nBytes.

The memory freed is mostly that of the page cache of the connections, which SQLite fills again when it needs the pages. The pages of an in-memory database are the database itself, and are never freed. The dbReleaseMemory method of the ooSQLiteConnection class frees the memory of a single connection. The method works because ooSQLite builds SQLite with the ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT option; without it, it would always return 0.
Raises a syntax error, 88.907, if nBytes is not a whole number that fits in 32 bits.
The functionality of the releaseMemory routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_release_memory API. The classic oosqlReleaseMemory routine does the same.

This example fills the cache with the pages of a new table, and then frees part of it. The numbers depend on the system and the version of SQLite:
sql = "CREATE TABLE notes(text); WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL" - "SELECT i + 1 FROM c WHERE i < 5000)" - "INSERT INTO notes SELECT hex(randomblob(200)) FROM c;" rc = db~exec(sql) rows = db~exec("SELECT count(*) FROM notes;", .true) -- the pages are in the cache now say 'In use: ' .ooSQLite~memoryUsed say 'Released:' .ooSQLite~releaseMemory(1000000) say 'In use: ' .ooSQLite~memoryUsed /* Output might be: In use: 2176360 Released: 1000272 In use: 1176088 */

section.title: softHeapLimit64 (Class method)
section.para: Sets or queries the soft limit on the amount of memory that SQLite uses.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
n [required]
The limit, in bytes. A positive number sets the limit, 0 removes it, and a negative number leaves it as it is, to query it.
The limit that was in place before the call, or 0 if there was none.

The limit is soft: when the memory in use approaches it, SQLite frees pages from its cache, but it exceeds the limit rather than fail. The limit applies to the whole process. By default there is no limit.
Raises a syntax error if n is not a whole number that fits in 64 bits.
The functionality of the softHeapLimit64 routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_soft_heap_limit64 API. The classic oosqlSoftHeapLimit64 routine does the same.

This example sets a limit of 8 megabytes, queries it, and restores the previous one:
old = .ooSQLite~softHeapLimit64(8 * 1024 * 1024) say 'Limit: ' .ooSQLite~softHeapLimit64(-1) .ooSQLite~softHeapLimit64(old) say 'Restored:' .ooSQLite~softHeapLimit64(-1) /* Output: Limit: 8388608 Restored: 0 */

section.title: sourceID (Class method)
section.para: Returns the source identifier of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
A string with the date and time of the check-in of the SQLite source code, and its SHA3-256 hash.

The source identifier tells exactly which SQLite source code was built, also between builds of the same version. It is the same as the SOURCE_ID constant of the ooSQLiteConstants class when ooSQLite.cls and the library belong together.
The functionality of the sourceID routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_sourceid API. The classic oosqlSourceID routine does the same.

This example displays the source identifier:
say .ooSQLite~sourceID /* Output might be: 2026-03-06 16:01:44 557aeb43869d3585137b17690cb3b64f7de6921774daae9e56403c3717dceab6 */

section.title: sqlite3Version (Class method)
section.para: Returns the version of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses, from the sqlite3_version string constant of SQLite.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The version, such as 3.52.0: the same string as libVersion returns.
SQLite keeps both because a program can be linked to one library and loaded with another; in ooSQLite, where SQLite is embedded, they are always equal.
The value is that of the SQLite sqlite3_version string constant, which SQLite defines besides the sqlite3_libversion API. The method is there for completeness.

This example shows that the two methods agree:
say .ooSQLite~sqlite3Version (.ooSQLite~sqlite3Version == .ooSQLite~libVersion) /* Output might be: 3.52.0 1 */

section.title: status (Class method)
section.para: Retrieves runtime status information about the performance of SQLite, and optionally resets its highwater mark.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
op [required]
The status parameter to retrieve, one of the Status Parameter constants, such as STATUS_MEMORY_USED.
result [required]
A Directory object, in which the values are returned. On success, it has two indexes: CURRENT, the current value of the parameter, and HIGHWATER, its highest recorded value.
reset [optional]
If true, the highwater mark is reset to the current value after it is retrieved. The default is false.
Returns OK on success, or MISUSE if op is not a valid status parameter. On error, the directory is not changed.

The values are for the whole process, not for a database connection: see the dbStatus method of the ooSQLiteConnection class for those. Some parameters do not record the highest value, and others record only the highest value; for parameters that do not record the highest value, reset is ignored.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if result is not a Directory object.
The functionality of the status routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_status API. The classic oosqlStatus routine does the same, with a stem instead of a directory.

This example displays how much memory SQLite is using, and how many allocations it has. The numbers depend on the system and the version of SQLite:
values = .directory~new if .ooSQLite~status(.ooSQLite~STATUS_MEMORY_USED, values) == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Memory used:' values['CURRENT'] 'bytes, highest:' values['HIGHWATER'] 'bytes' if .ooSQLite~status(.ooSQLite~STATUS_MALLOC_COUNT, values) == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Allocations:' values['CURRENT']', highest:' values['HIGHWATER'] /* Output might be: Memory used: 63688 bytes, highest: 63712 bytes Allocations: 136, highest: 137 */

section.title: &added11;strGlob (Class method)
section.para: Tests if a string matches a pattern, with the rules of the GLOB operator of SQLite.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
glob [required]
The pattern. * matches any sequence of characters, ? any single character, and [...] any of the characters between the brackets, which can include ranges such as a-z.
str [required]
The string to test.
Returns 0 if the string matches the pattern, and a number that is not 0 if it does not. Note that 0, which is false in Rexx, means a match.
The comparison is case sensitive, as the GLOB operator is: *.txt does not match a.TXT. The return value follows the convention of string comparison functions in C, where 0 means equal.
The functionality of the strGlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_strglob API. The classic oosqlStrGlob routine does the same.
&added11;This method was in ooSQLite before version 1.1, but it was not documented.

This example displays the names that start with Ba or ba:
do name over .array~of('Bagels', 'Bacon', 'bread', 'Cheese') if .ooSQLite~strGlob('[Bb]a*', name) == 0 then say name end /* Output: Bagels Bacon */

section.title: threadSafe (Class method)
section.para: Tells whether the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses was built with support for threads.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.

The value of the SQLITE_THREADSAFE compile-time option: 0 if the library was built without support for threads, 1 for the serialized threading mode, 2 for the multi-thread mode. ooSQLite builds SQLite with the value 1, so the method returns 1.

The value is the default threading mode. The mode can be changed when a connection is opened, with the OPEN_NOMUTEX and OPEN_FULLMUTEX flags of the new method of the ooSQLiteConnection class, but not to or from 0.
The functionality of the threadSafe routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_threadsafe API. The classic oosqlThreadSafe routine does the same.

This example displays the threading mode:
say 'Threading mode:' .ooSQLite~threadSafe /* Output: Threading mode: 1 */

section.title: version (Class method)
section.para: Returns the version of ooSQLite, or of the SQLite library it uses, in one of several formats.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
type [optional]
The format, one of these keywords. Only the first letter is checked, and case is not significant: OneLine, the version of ooSQLite on one line, such as ooSQLite Version 1.0.2.13107 (64 bit), the default; Compact, the version number of ooSQLite, such as 1.0.2.13107; Full, several lines, with the versions of ooSQLite, ooRexx, and SQLite, the date ooSQLite was built, and its copyright; LibVersion, the version of SQLite, as libVersion returns it; Number, the version of SQLite as a number, as libVersionNumber returns it; and SourceID, the source identifier of SQLite, as sourceID returns it.
The version, in the format asked for.

This is the method that returns the version of ooSQLite. The Full format is useful in problem reports. Since a method takes precedence over a constant, .ooSQLite~VERSION invokes this method, and not the VERSION constant: see libVersion.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if type does not start with one of the letters O, C, F, L, N, or S.
This method is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API. The classic ooSQLiteVersion routine does the same.

This example displays the version in several formats. The output depends on the build:
say .ooSQLite~version say .ooSQLite~version('Compact') say .ooSQLite~version('LibVersion') say .ooSQLite~version('F') /* Output might be: ooSQLite Version 1.0.2.13107 (64 bit) 1.0.2.13107 3.52.0 ooSQLite: ooSQLite Version 1.0.2.13107 (64 bit) Built Oct 18 2026 13:47:21 Copyright (c) 2012-2026 Rexx Language Association. All rights reserved.
Rexx: Open Object Rexx Version 5.3.0
SQLite: SQLite Library Version 3.52.0 2026-03-06 16:01:44 */
